vacant.etymology: F., fr. L. vacans, -antis, p. pr. of vacare to be empty, to be free or unoccupied, to have leisure, also vocare; akin to vacuus empty, and probably to E. void. Cf. Evacuate, Void, a.

vacate.etymology: L. vacare, vacatum, to be empty. See Vacant.

vacation.etymology: F., fr. L. vacatio a being free from a duty, service, etc., fr. vacare. See Vacate.

vaccine.etymology: L. vaccinus, fr. vacca a cow; cf. Skr. vac to bellow, to groan.

vacillant.etymology: L. vacillans, p. pr. of vacillare: cf. F. vacillant. See Vacillate.

vacillate.etymology: L. vacillare, vacillatum; cf. Skr. vañc.

vacuole.etymology: L. vacuus empty: cf. F. vacuole.

vacuum.etymology: L., fr. vacuus empty. See Vacuous.

vagabond.etymology: F., fr. L. vagabundus, from vagari to stroll about, from vagus strolling. See Vague.

vagary.etymology: L. vagari to stroll about. See Vague.

vagina.etymology: L. vagina a scabbard or sheath.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

vagrant.etymology: Probably fr. OF. waucrant, wacrant, p. p. of waucrer, wacrer, walcrer, to wander (probably of Teutonic origin), but influenced by F. vagant, p. pr. of vaguer to stray, L. vagari. Cf. Vagary.

vague.etymology: F. vague, or L. vagus. See Vague, v. i.

vain.etymology: F. vain, L. vanus empty, void, vain. Cf. Vanish, Vanity, Vaunt to boast.

valance.etymology: Perhaps fr. OF. avalant descending, hanging down, p. pr. of avaler to go down, let down, descent (cf. Avalanche); but probably from the town of Valence in France.

vale.etymology: OE. val, F. val, L. vallis; perhaps akin to Gr. Avalanche, Vail to lower, Valley.

valediction.etymology: L., valedicere, valedictum, to say farewell; vale farewell (imperative of valere to be strong or well) + dicere to say. See Valiant, Diction.

valence.etymology: From L. valens, -entis, p. pr. of valere to have power, to be strong. See Valiant.

valerian.etymology: LL. valeriana, perhaps from some person named Valerius, or fr. L. valere to be strong. powerful, on account of its medicinal virtues: cf. F. valériane.

valet.etymology: F. valet, OF. vallet, varlet, vaslet. See Varlet, and Vassal.

valetudinarian.etymology: L. valetudinarius, from valetudo state of health, health, ill health, fr. valere to be strong or well: cf. F. valétudinaire. See Valiant.

valhalla.etymology: Icel. valhöll, literally, hall of the slain; valr the slain (akin to AS. wæl, OHG. wal battlefield, wuol defeat, slaughter, AS. wol pestilence) + höll a royal hall. See Hall, and cf. Walhalla.

valiant.etymology: OE. valiant, F. vaillant, OF. vaillant, valant, originally p. pr. of OF. & F. valoir to be worth, L. valere to be strong. See Wield, and cf. Avail, Convalesce, Equivalent, Prevail, Valid.

valid.etymology: F. valide, F. validus strong, from valere to be strong. See Valiant.

validity.etymology: Cf. F. validité, L. validitas strength.

valise.etymology: F. valise; cf. It. valigia, Sp. balija, LL. valisia, valesia; of uncertain origin, perhaps through (assumed) LL. vidulitia, from L. vidulus a leathern trunk; a knapsack.

vallecula.etymology: NL., dim. fr. L. vallis, valles, a valley.

valley.etymology: OE. vale, valeie, OF. valée, valede, F. vallée, LL. vallata, L. vallis, valles. See Vale.

valor.etymology: OE. valour, OF. valor, valur, valour, F. valeur, LL. valor, fr. L. valere to be strong, or worth. See Valiant.

value.etymology: OF. value, fr. valoir, p. p. valu, to be worth, fr. L. valere to be strong, to be worth. See Valiant.

valve.etymology: L. valva the leaf, fold, or valve of a door: cf. F. valve.

valvula.etymology: NL., dim. fr. L. valva fold, valve of a door.

vamp.etymology: OE. vampe, vaumpe, vauntpe, F. avantpied the forefoot, vamp; anat before, fore + pied foot, L. pes. See Advance, Van of an army, and Foot.

vampire.etymology: F. vampire (cf. It. vampiro, G. & D. vampir), fr. Servian vampir.

vanadium.etymology: NL., fr. Icel. Vanadis, a surname of the Scandinavian goddess Freya.

vandal.etymology: L. Vandalus, Vandalius; of Teutonic origin, and probably originally signifying, a wanderer. Cf. Wander.

vane.etymology: OE. & E. Prov. E. fane weathercock, banner, AS. fana a banner, flag; akin to D. vaan, G. fahne, OHG. fano cloth, gund fano flag, Icel. fani, Sw. fana, Dan. fane, Goth. fana cloth, L. pannus, and perhaps to Gr.Fanon, Pane a compartment, panel.

vanessa.etymology: Probably from Swift's poem of Cadenus and Vanessa. See Vanessa, in the Dictionary of Noted Names in Fiction.

vanguard.etymology: For vantguard, avantguard, F. avant-garde; avant before, fore + garde guard. See Avant, Ab-,Ante-, and Guard, and cf. Advance, Vamp, Van of an army, Vaward.

roots.meaning: A prefix in many words of Latin origin. It signifies from, away , separating, or departure, as in abduct, abstract, abscond. See A- (6).

A Latin preposition and prefix; akin to Gr. anti, Goth. and-, anda- (only in comp.), AS. and-, ond-, (only in comp.: cf. Answer, Along), G. ant-, ent- (in comp.). The Latin ante is generally used in the sense of before, in regard to position, order, or time, and the Gr. opposite, or in the place of.

vanilla.etymology: NL., fr. Sp. vainilla, dim. of Sp. vaina a sheath, a pod, L. vagina; because its grains, or seeds, are contained in little pods.

vanish.etymology: OE. vanissen, OF. vanir (in comp.): cf. OF. envanir, esvanir, esvanuïr, F. s'évanouir; fr. L. vanus empty, vain; cf. L. vanescere, evanescere, to vanish. See Vain, and cf. Evanescent,-ish.

vanity.etymology: OE. vanite, vanité, L. vanitas, fr. vanus empty, vain. See Vain.

vanquish.etymology: OE. venquishen, venquissen, venkisen,F. vaincre, pret. vainquis, OF. veintre, pret. venqui, venquis (cf. an OF. infin. vainquir), fr. L. vincere; akin to AS. wig war, battle, wigant a warrior, wigan to fight, Icel. vig battle, Goth. weihan to fight, contend. Cf. Convince, Evict, Invincible, Victor.

vantage.etymology: Aphetic form of OE. avantage,fr. F. avantage. See Advantage.

vapid.etymology: L. vapidus having lost its lire and spirit, vapid; akin to vappa vapid wine, vapor vapor. See Vapor.

vapor.etymology: OE. vapour, OF. vapour, vapor, vapeur, F. vapeur, L. vapor; probably for cvapor, and akin to Gr. kvepti to breathe, smell, Russ. kopote fine soot. Cf. Vapid.

vaporific.etymology: L. vapor vapor + facere to make.

vaquero.etymology: Sp., cowherd, fr. vaca a cow, L. vacca. Cf. Vacher.

varanus.etymology: NL., fr. Ar. waran, waral; cf. F. varan, from the Arabic.

variant.etymology: L. varians, p. pr. of variare to change: cf. F. variant. See Vary.

variate.etymology: L. variatus, p. p. of variare. See Vary.

variation.etymology: OE. variatioun, F. variation, L. variatio. See Vary.

varicella.etymology: NL., dim. of LL. variola smallpox.

varicocele.etymology: Varix a dilated vein + Gr. varicocèle.

varicose.etymology: L. varicosus, from varix, -icis, a dilated vein; cf. varus bent, stretched, crooked.

variegate.etymology: L. variegatus, p. p. of variegare to variegate; varius various + agere to move, make. See Various, and Agent.

variety.etymology: L. varietas: cf. F. variété. See Various.

variola.etymology: LL., fr. L. varius various. See Various.

variolous.etymology: LL. variolosus, fr. variola the smallpox: cf. F. varioleux.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

variorum.etymology: L., abbrev. fr. cum notis variorum with notes of various persons.

varlet.etymology: OF. varlet, vaslet, vallet, servant, young man, young noble, dim of vassal. See Vassal, and cf. Valet.

varnish.etymology: OE. vernish, F. vernis, LL. vernicium; akin to F. vernir to varnish, fr. (assumed) LL. vitrinire to glaze, from LL. vitrinus glassy, fr. L. vitrum glass. See Vitreous.

vary.etymology: OE. varien, F. varier, L. variare, fr. varius various. See Various, and cf. Variate.

vascular.etymology: L. vasculum a small vessel, dim. of vas vessel: cf. F. vasculaire. See Vase, and cf. Vessel.

vase.etymology: F. vase; cf. Sp. & It. vaso; fr. L. vas, vasum. Cf. Vascular, Vessel.

vaseline.etymology: Said by the manufacturer to be derived from G. wasser water + Gr. 'e`laion olive oil.

vasomotor.etymology: L. vas a vessel + motor that which moves fr. movere to move.

vassal.etymology: F., fr. LL. vassallus, vassus; of Celtic origin; cf. W. & Corn. gwas a youth, page, servant, Arm. gwaz a man, a male. Cf. Valet, Varlet, Vavasor.

vassalage.etymology: OE. vassalage, F. vasselage, LL. vassallaticum.

vast.etymology: L. vastus empty, waste, enormous, immense: cf. F. vaste. See Waste, and cf. Devastate.

vat.etymology: A dialectic form for fat, OE. fat, AS. fæt; akin to D.vat, OS. fat, G. fass, OHG. faz, Icel. & Sw. fat, Dan.fad, Lith. p a pot, and probably to G. fassen to seize, to contain, OHG. fazz, D. vatten. Cf. Fat a vat.

vatican.etymology: L. Vaticanus, mons, or collis, Vaticanus, the Vatican hill, in Rome, on the western bank of the Tiber: cf. F. Vatican, It. Vaticano.

vaticinate.etymology: L. vaticinatus, p. p. of vaticinari to prophesy, fr. vaticinus prophetical, fr. vates a prophet.

vaudeville.etymology: F., fr. Vau-de-vire, a village in Normandy, where Olivier Basselin, at the end of the 14th century, composed such songs.

vault.etymology: OE. voute, OF. voute, volte, F. voûte, LL. volta, for voluta, volutio, fr. L. volvere, volutum, to roll, to turn about. See Voluble, and cf. Vault a leap, Volt a turn, Volute.

vaunt.etymology: F. vanter, LL. vanitare, fr. L. vanus vain. See Vain.

veal.etymology: OE. veel, OF. veel, F. veau, L. vitellus, dim. of vitulus a calf; akin to E. wether. See Wether, and cf. Vellum, Vituline.

vector.etymology: L., a bearer, carrier. fr. vehere, vectum, to carry.

veda.etymology: Skr. v, properly, knowledge, from vid to know. See Wit.

veer.etymology: F. virer (cf. Sp. virar, birar), LL. virare; perhaps fr. L. vibrare to brandish, vibrate (cf. Vibrate); or cf. L. viriae armlets, bracelets, viriola a little bracelet (cf. Ferrule). Cf. Environ.

vega.etymology: Ar. w, properly, falling: cf. F. Wéga.

vegetable.etymology: F. végétable growing, capable of growing, formerly also, as a noun, a vegetable, from L. vegetabilis enlivening, from vegetare to enliven, invigorate, quicken, vegetus enlivened, vigorous, active, vegere to quicken, arouse, to be lively, akin to vigere to be lively, to thrive, vigil watchful, awake, and probably to E. wake, v. See Vigil, Wake, v.

vegetate.etymology: L. vegetatus, p. p. of vegetare to enliven. See Vegetable.

vegetation.etymology: Cf. F. végétation, L. vegetatio an enlivening. See Vegetable.

vehement.etymology: L. vehemens, the first part of which is perhaps akin to vehere to carry, and the second mens mind: cf. F. véhément. Cf. Vehicle, and Mental.

vehicle.etymology: L. vehiculum, fr. vehere to carry; akin to E. way, wain. See Way, n., and cf. Convex, Inveigh, Veil, Vex.

veil.etymology: OE. veile, OF. veile, F. voile, L. velum a sail, covering, curtain, veil, probably fr. vehere to bear, carry, and thus originally, that which bears the ship on. See Vehicle, and cf. Reveal.

vein.etymology: OE. veine, F. veine, L. vena.

velleity.etymology: F. velléité (cf. It. velleità), fr. L. velle to will, to be willing.

vellicate.etymology: L. vellicatus, p. p. of vellicare to twitch, fr. vellere to pluck, pull.

vellum.etymology: OE. velim, F. vélin, fr. L. vitulinus of a calf, fr. vitulus a calf. See Veal.

velocipede.etymology: L. velox, -ocis, swift + pes, pedis, a foot. See Velocity, and Foot.

velocity.etymology: L. velocitas, from velox, - ocis, swift, quick; perhaps akin to v to fly (see Volatile): cf. F. vélocité.

velum.etymology: L., an awning, a veil. See Veil.

velvet.etymology: OE. velouette, veluet, velwet; cf. OF. velluau, LL. velluetum, vellutum, It. velluto, Sp. velludo; all fr. (assumed) LL. villutus shaggy, fr L. villus shaggy hair; akin to vellus a fleece, and E. wool. See Wool, and cf. Villous.

vend.etymology: F. vendre, L. vendere, from venum dare; venus sale + dare to give. See 2d Venal, Date, time.

vender.etymology: From Vend: cf. F. vendeur, OF. vendeor. Cf. Vendor.

vendible.etymology: L. vendibilis: cf. OF. vendible, F. vendable.

vendue.etymology: OF. vendue, from F. vendre, p. p. vendu, vendue, to sell.

veneer.etymology: G. furnieren, fourniren, fr. F. fournir to furnish. See Furnish.

venerate.etymology: L. veneratus, p. p. of venerari to venerate; akin to Venus Venus, Skr. van to like, to wish, and E. winsome. See Winsome.

venereal.etymology: L. venereus, venerius, fr. Venus, Veneris, Venus, the goddess of love. See Venerate.

venesection.etymology: NL. venaesectio; L. vena vein + sectio section.

vengeance.etymology: F. vengeance, fr. venger to avenge, L. vindicare to lay claim to, defend, avenge, fr. vindex a claimant, defender, avenger, the first part of which is of uncertain origin, and the last part akin to dicere to say. See Diction, and cf. Avenge, Revenge, Vindicate.

venial.etymology: OF. venial, F. véniel, L. venialis, from venia forgiveness, pardon, grace, favor, kindness; akin to venerari to venerate. See Venerate.

venison.etymology: OE. veneison, veneson, venison, OF. veneison, F. venaison, L. venatio hunting, the chase, game, fr. venari, p. p. venatus, to hunt; perhaps akin to OHG. weidin, weidenen, to pasture, to hunt, G. weide pasturage. Cf. Gain to acquire, Venation.

venom.etymology: OE. venim, OF. venim, F. venin, L. veneum. Cf. Venenate.

venomous.etymology: OE. venemous, venimous, F. venimeux, L. venenosus, fr. venenum poison. See Venom, and cf. Venenose.

venous.etymology: L. venosus, from vena a vein. See Vein.

vent.etymology: F. vente, fr. L. vendere, -itum, to sell; perh. confused with E. vent an opening. See Vend.

ventail.etymology: OF. ventaille, F. ventail. See Ventilate, and cf. Aventail.

ventilate.etymology: L. ventilatus, p. p. of ventilare to toss, brandish in the air, to fan, to winnow, from ventus wind; akin to E. wind. See Wind rushing air.

ventilator.etymology: Cf. F. ventilateur, L. ventilator a winnower.

ventral.etymology: L. ventralis, fr. venter the belly; perhaps akin to G. wanst: cf. F. ventral.

ventricle.etymology: L. ventriculus the stomach, a ventricle, dim. of venter the belly: cf. F. ventricule. See Ventral.

ventricose.etymology: NL. ventricosus, fr. L. venter belly.

ventricous.etymology: NL. ventricosus, fr. L. venter belly.

ventriculus.etymology: L., belly, dim. fr. venter belly.

venture.etymology: Aphetic form of OE. aventure. See Adventure.

venturous.etymology: Aphetic form of OE. aventurous. See Adventurous, Venture, n.

venue.etymology: F. venue a coming, arrival, fr. venir to come, L. venire; hence, in English, the place whither the jury are summoned to come. See Come, and cf. Venew, Veney.

venule.etymology: L. venula, dim. from vena vein.

venus.etymology: L. Venus, -eris, the goddess of love, the planet Venus.

veracious.etymology: L. verax, -acis, fr. verus true. See Very.

veranda.etymology: A word brought by the English from India; of uncertain origin; cf. Skr. vara, Pg. varanda, Sp. baranda, Malay baranda.

verb.etymology: F. verbe, L. verbum a word, verb. See Word.

verbal.etymology: F., fr. L. verbalis. See Verb.

verbiage.etymology: F. verbiage, from OF. verbe a word. See Verb.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

verbose.etymology: L. verbosus, from verbum a word. See Verb.

verdant.etymology: F. verdoyant, p. pr. of verdoyer to be verdant, to grow green, OF. verdoier, verdeier, fr. verd, vert, green, fr. L. viridis green, fr. virere to be green: cf. OF. verdant verdant, L. viridans, p. pr. of viridare to make green. Cf. Farthingale, Verjuice, Vert.

verdict.etymology: OE. verdit, OF. verdit, veirdit, LL. verdictum, veredictum; L. vere truly (fr. verus true) + dictum a saying, a word, fr. dicere, dictum, to say. See Very, and Dictum.

verdigris.etymology: F. vert-de-gris, apparently from verd, vert, green + de of + gris gray, but really a corruption of LL. viride aeris (equivalent to L. aerugo), from L. viridis green + aes, aeris, brass. See Verdant, and 2d Ore.

verdin.etymology: Cf. Sp. verdino bright green, F. verdin the yellow-hammer.

verdure.etymology: F., fr. L. viridis green. See Verdant.

verge.etymology: F. verge, L. virga; perhaps akin to E. wisp.

verger.etymology: F. verger, from verge a rod. See 1st Verge.

veridical.etymology: L. veridicus; verus true + dicere to say, tell.

verify.etymology: F. vérifier, LL. verificare, from L. verus true + -ficare to make. See Very, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

verisimilar.etymology: L. verisimilis; verus true + similis like, similar. See Very, and Similar.

verisimilitude.etymology: L. verisimilitudo: cf. OF. verisimilitude. See Verisimilar.

verity.etymology: F. vérité, L. veritas, fr. verus true. See Very.

vermicelli.etymology: It., pl. of vermicello, literally, a little worm, dim. of verme a worm, L. vermis. See Worm, and cf. Vermicule, Vermeil.

vermicide.etymology: L. vermis a worm + caedere to kill.

vermicular.etymology: L. vermiculus a little worm, dim. of vermis a worm: cf. F. vermiculaire. See Vermicelli.

vermiculate.etymology: L. vermiculatus inlaid so as to resemble the tracks of worms, p. p. of vermiculari to be full of worms, vermiculus a little worm. See Vermicular.

vermiculite.etymology: L. vermiculus, dim. of vermis worm.

vermin.etymology: OE. vermine, F. vermine, from L. vermis a worm; cf. LL. vermen a worm, L. verminosus full of worms. See Vermicular, Worm.

verminous.etymology: L. verminosus, fr. vermis a worm: cf. F. vermineux.

vernacular.etymology: L. vernaculus born in one's house, native, fr. verna a slave born in his master's house, a native, probably akin to Skr. vas to dwell, E. was.

vernal.etymology: L. vernalis, fr. vernus vernal, ver spring; akin to Gr. vasanta, Icel. var, and E. Easter, east.

vernation.etymology: F. vernation: cf. L. vernatio the sloughing of the skin of snakes.

vernier.etymology: So named after the inventor, Pierre Vernier.

verrucose.etymology: L. verrucosus, fr. verruca a wart.

versant.etymology: L. versans, p. pr. versare to turn abound frequently, to turn over in the mind, to meditate. See Versatile.

versatile.etymology: L. versatilis, fr. versare to turn around, v. freq. of vertere: cf. F. versatile. See Verse.

verse.etymology: OE. vers, AS. fers, L. versus a line in writing, and, in poetry, a verse, from vertere, versum, to turn, to turn round; akin to E. worth to become: cf. F. vers. See Worth to become, and cf. Advertise, Averse, Controversy, Convert, Divers, Invert, Obverse, Prose, Suzerain, Vortex.

versed.etymology: Cf. F. versé, L. versatus, p. p. of versari to turn about frequently, to turn over, to be engaged in a thing, passive of versare. See Versant, a.

versicle.etymology: L. versiculus, dim. of versus. See Verse.

versify.etymology: OE. versifien, F. versifier, L. versificare; versus a verse + -ficare to make. See Verse, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

version.etymology: F., from L. vertere, versum, to turn, to change, to translate. See Verse.

verso.etymology: L. versus, p. p. of vertere to turn: cf. F. verso.

vertebra.etymology: L. vertebra, fr. vertere to turn, change. See Verse.

vertex.etymology: L. vertex, -icis, a whirl, top of the head, top, summit, from vertere to turn. See Verse, and cf. Vortex.

verticil.etymology: L. verticillus, dim. of vertex a whirl: cf. F. verticille. See Vertex.

vertiginous.etymology: L. vertiginosus, fr. vertigo a whirling around, giddiness: cf. F. vertigineux. See Vertig.

vertigo.etymology: L., fr. vertere to turn. See Verse.

vervain.etymology: OE. verveine, F. verveine, fr. L. verbena, pl. verbenae sacred boughs of laurel, olive, or myrtle, a class of plants; cf. verbenaca vervain. Cf. Verbena.

very.etymology: OE. verai, verray, OF. verai, vrai, F. vrai, (assumed) LL. veracus, for L. verax true, veracious, fr. verus true; akin to OHG. & OS. war, G. wahr, D. waar; perhaps originally, that is or exists, and akin to E. was. Cf. Aver, v. t., Veracious, Verdict, Verity.

vesicant.etymology: L. vesica blister: cf. F. vésicant.

vesicle.etymology: L. vesicula, dim. of vesica a bladder, blister; akin to Skr. vasti bladder: cf. F. vésicule.

vesper.etymology: L., the evening, the evening star, the west; akin to Gr. west. Cf. Hesperian, Vespers.

vespers.etymology: OF. vespres, F. vêpres, LL. vesperae, fr. L. vespera evening. See Vesper, n.

vessel.etymology: OF. vessel, veissel, vaissel, vaissiel, F. vascellum, dim. of vasculum, dim. of vas a vessel. Cf. Vascular, Vase.

vest.etymology: L. vestis a garment, vesture; akin to Goth. wasti, and E. wear: cf. F. veste. See Wear to carry on the person, and cf. Divest, Invest, Travesty.

vesta.etymology: L. Vesta, akin to Gr. ush to burn (see East), or perhaps to Skr. vas to dwell, and E. was.

vestal.etymology: L. Vestalis belonging to Vesta, vestal. See Vesta.

vestibule.etymology: L. vestibulum, of uncertain origin: cf. F. vestibule.

vestige.etymology: F., from L. vestigium footprint, trace, sign; the last part (-stigium) is probably akin to E. sty, v. i. Cf. Investigate.

vestment.etymology: OE. vestement, vestiment, OF. vestement, vestiment, F. vêtement, fr. L. vestimentum, fr. vestire to clothe, fr. vestis a garment, clothing. See Vest.

vestry.etymology: OE. vestrye, F. vestiaire, L. vestiarium, fr. vestiarius belonging to clothes, fr. vestis a garment. See Vest, n., and cf. Vestiary.

vesture.etymology: OF. vesture, vesteure, F. vêture, LL. vestitura, from L. vestire to clothe, dress. See Vest, v. t., and cf. Vestiture.

vetch.etymology: Also fitch; OE. ficche, feche, for veche, OF. veche, vecce, vesche, vesce, F. vesce, fr. L. vicia.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

veteran.etymology: L. veteranus, from vetus, veteris, old; akin to Gr. vatsara. See Wether.

veterinary.etymology: L. veterinarius of or belonging to beasts of burden an draught, fr. veterinus, probably originally, of or pertaining to yearlings: cf. F. vétérinaire. See Veteran, Wether.

vex.etymology: F. vexer, L. vexare, vexatum, to vex, originally, to shake, toss, in carrying, v. intens. fr. vehere, vectum, to carry. See Vehicle.

viable.etymology: F., from vie life, L. vita. See Vital.

viaduct.etymology: L. via a way + -duct, as in aqueduct: cf. F. viaduc. See Via, and Aqueduct.

vial.etymology: OE. viole, fiole, F. fiole. See Phial.

viand.etymology: F. viande meat, food, LL. vianda, vivanda, vivenda, properly, things to live on, fr. L. vivere to live; akin to vivus living. See Vivid, and cf. Victualis.

vibrant.etymology: L. vibrans, p. pr.: cf. F. vibrant. See Vibrate.

vibrate.etymology: L. vibratus, p. p. of vibrare, v. t. & v. i., to snake, brandish, vibrate; akin to Skr. vip to tremble, Icel. veifa to wave, vibrate. See Waive and cf. Whip, v. t.

vibrio.etymology: NL., fr. L. vibrare to vibrate, to move by undulations.

vibrissa.etymology: L. vibrissae, pl., the hairs in the nostrils of man, fr. vibrare to vibrate; -- so called because touching them tickles a person, and causes him to shake his head.

vicar.etymology: OE. vicar, viker, vicair, F. vicaire, fr. L. vicarius. See Vicarious.

vicarious.etymology: L. vicarius, from vicis change, alternation, turn, the position, place, or office of one person as assumed by another; akin to Gr. wechsel a change, and probably also to E. weak. See Weak, and cf. Vice, prep.

vicegerent.etymology: Vice, a + gerent: cf. F. vicegérant.

vicenary.etymology: L. vicenarius, fr. viceni twenty each; akin to viginti twenty.

vicennial.etymology: L. vicennium a period of twenty years; viceni twenty + annus year.

viceroy.etymology: F. vice-roi; pref. vice- in the place of (L. vice) + roi a king, L. rex. See Vice, prep. and Royal.

vicinity.etymology: L. vicinitas, from vicinus neighboring, near, from vicus a row of houses, a village; akin to Gr. v a house, vi to enter, Goth. weihs town: cf. OF. vicinité. Cf. Diocese, Economy, Parish, Vicinage, Wick a village.

vicious.etymology: OF. vicious, F. vicieux, fr. L. vitiosus, fr. vitium vice. See Vice a fault.

vicissitude.etymology: L. vicissitudo, fr. vicis change, turn: cf. F. vicissitude. See Vicarious.

victor.etymology: L. victor, fr. vincere, victum, to vanquish, to conquer. See Vanquish.

victorious.etymology: L. victoriosus: cf. F. victorieux. See Victory.

victory.etymology: OE. victorie, OF. victorie, victoire, F. victoire, L. victoria. See Victor.

victuals.etymology: OE. vitaille, OF. vitaille, F. victuaille, pl. victuailles, fr. L. victualia, pl. of. victualis belonging to living or nourishment, fr. victus nourishment, from vivere, victum, to live; akin to vivus living. See Vivid.

videlicet.etymology: L., contr. fr. videre licet, literally, it is easy to see, one may or can see.

vie.etymology: OE. vien, shortened fr. envien, OF. envier to invite, to challenge, a word used in gambling, L. invitare to invite; of uncertain origin. Cf. Invite, Envie.

view.etymology: OF. veue, F. vue, fr. OF. veoir to see, p. p. veu, F. voir, p. p. vu, fr. L. videre to see. See Vision, and cl. Interview, Purview, Review, Vista.

vigesimal.etymology: L. vigesimus twentieth, from viginti twenty.

vigil.etymology: OE. vigile, L. vigilia, from vigil awake, watchful, probably akin to E. wake: cf. F. vigile. See Wake, v. i., and cf. Reveille, Surveillance, Vedette, Vegetable, Vigor.

vigilant.etymology: L. vigilans, -antis, p. pr. of vigilare to watch, fr. vigil awake: cf. F. vigilant. See Vigil.

vignette.etymology: F. vignette, fr. vigne a vine. See Vine, and cf. Vinette.

vigor.etymology: OE. vigour, vigor, OF. vigor, vigur, vigour, F. vigueur, fr. L. vigor, fr. vigere to be lively or strong. See Vegetable, Vigil.

vigorous.etymology: Cf. OF. vigoros, F. vigoureux, LL. vigorosus.

viking.etymology: Icel. vikingr, fr. vik a bay, inlet.

vile.etymology: OE. vil, F. vil, from L. vilis cheap, worthless, vile, base.

vilify.etymology: L. vilis vile + -fly; cf. L. vilificare to esteem of little value.

vilipend.etymology: L. vilipendere; vilis vile + pendere to weigh, to value: cf. F. vilipender.

villa.etymology: L. villa, LL. also village, dim. of L. vicus a village: cf. It. & F. villa. See Vicinity, and cf. Vill, Village, Villain.

village.etymology: F., fr. L. villaticus belonging to a country house or villa. See Villa, and cf. Villatic.

villain.etymology: OE. vilein, F. vilain, LL. villanus, from villa a village, L. villa a farm. See Villa.

villainy.etymology: OE. vilanie, OF. vilanie, vilainie, vileinie, vilanie, LL. villania. See Villain, n.

villus.etymology: L., shaggy hair, a tuft of hair.

vincible.etymology: L. vincibilis, fr. vincere to vanquish, conquer: cf. F. vincible. See Victor.

vindicate.etymology: L. vindicatus, p. p. of vindicare to lay claim to, defend, avenge. See Vengeance.

vindication.etymology: L. vindicatio a laying claim, defense, vindication. See Vindicate.

vindictive.etymology: For vindicative, confused with L. vindicta revenge, punishment, fr. vindicare to vindicate. Cf. Vindicative.

vine.etymology: F. vigne, L. vinea a vineyard, vine from vineus of or belonging to wine, vinum wine, grapes. See Wine, and cf. Vignette.

vinegar.etymology: OE. vinegre, F. vinaigre; vin wine (L. vinum) + aigre sour. See Wine, and Eager, a.

vineyard.etymology: For OE. winyard, AS. wingeard; influenced by E. vine. See Wine, and Yard an inclosure.

vinous.etymology: L. vinosus, fr. vinum wine: cf. F. vineux. See Wine.

vintage.etymology: Corrupted by influence of vintner, vintry, from OE. vindage, vendage, for vendange, OF. vendenge, F. vendange, from L. vindemia; vinum wine, grapes + demere to take off; de + emere, originally, to take. See Wine, Redeem, and cf. Vindemial.

vintner.etymology: OE. vintener, viniter, OF. vinetier, vinotier, LL. vinetarius, fr. L. vinetum a vineyard, fr. vinum wine. See Wine.

roots.meaning: A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc.

viol.etymology: F. viole; cf. Pr. viola, viula, Sp., Pg., & It. viola, LL. vitula; of uncertain origin; perhaps from L. vitulari to celebrate a festival, keep holiday, be joyful, perhaps originally, to sacrifice a calf (vitulus; cf. Veal). Cf. Fiddle, Vielle, 2d Viola, Violin.

violable.etymology: L. violabilis: cf. F. violable. See Violate.

violate.etymology: L. violatus, p. p. of violare to violate, fr. vis strength, force. See Violent.

violence.etymology: F., fr. L. violentia. See Violent.

violet.etymology: F. violette a violet (cf. violet violet-colored), dim. of OF. viole a violet, L. viola; akin to Gr. Iodine.

violin.etymology: It. violino, dim. of viola. See Viol.

violinist.etymology: Cf. F. violiniste, violoniste, It. violonista.

violoncello.etymology: It. violoncello, dim. of violone a bass viol. See Violone.

viper.etymology: F. vipère, L. vipera, probably contr. fr. vivipera; vivus alive + parere to bring forth, because it was believed to be the only serpent that brings forth living young. Cf. Quick, a., Parent, Viviparous, Wivern, Weever.

virago.etymology: L. virago, -intis, from vir a man. See Virile.

virgin.etymology: L. virgo, -inis: cf. OF. virgine, virgene, virge, vierge, F. vierge.

virginity.etymology: OE. virgintee, F. virginité, L. virginitas.

virgo.etymology: L. virgo a virgin, the constellation Virgo in the zodiac. See Virgin.

virgule.etymology: F. virgule, fr. L. virgula, dim. of virga. See Verge a rod.

viridity.etymology: L. viriditas, fr. viridis green: cf. F. viridité. See Verdant.

virile.etymology: L. virilis, fr. vir a man; akin to AS. wer: cf. F. viril. See Werewolf, World, and cf. Decemvir, Virago, Virtue.

virtu.etymology: It. virtù virtue, excellence, from L. virtus. See Virtue.

virtue.etymology: OE. vertu, F. vertu, L. virtus strength, courage, excellence, virtue, fr. vir a man. See Virile, and cf. Virtu.

virtuous.etymology: OE. vertuous, OF. vertuos, vertuous, F. vertueux, fr. L. Virtuous. See Virtue, and cf. Virtuoso.

virulence.etymology: Cf. F. virulence, L. virulentia an offensive odor, a stench.

virulency.etymology: Cf. F. virulence, L. virulentia an offensive odor, a stench.

virulent.etymology: L. virulentus, fr. virus poison: cf. F. virulent. See Virus.

virus.etymology: L., a slimy liquid, a poisonous liquid, poison, stench; akin to Gr. visha. Cf. Wizen, v. i.

visage.etymology: F. visage, from L. visus a seeing, a look, fr. videre, visum, to see. See Vision.

viscid.etymology: L. viscidus, fr. viscum the mistletoe, birdlime made from the berries of the mistletoe; akin to Gr. viscide.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

viscount.etymology: OE. vicounte, OF. visconte, vescunte, F. vicomte, LL. vicecomes; L. vice (see Vice, a.) + comes a companion, LL., a count. See Count.

viscus.etymology: L., perhaps akin to E. viscid.

vise.etymology: F. vis a screw, winding stairs, OF. vis, viz, fr. L. vitis a vine; probably akin to E. withy.

vishnu.etymology: Skr. Vish, from vish to pervade., to extend through nature.

visible.etymology: L. visibilis, fr. videre, visum, to see: cf. F. visible. See Vision.

visigoth.etymology: L. Visegothae, pl. Cf. West, and Goth.

vision.etymology: OE. visioun, F. vision, fr. L. visio, from videre, visum, to see: akin to Gr. wit. See Wit, v., and cf. Advice, Clairvoyant, Envy, Evident, Provide, Revise, Survey, View, Visage, Visit.

visit.etymology: F. visiter, L. visitare, fr. visere to go to see, to visit, fr. videre, visum to see. See Vision.

visitant.etymology: L. visitans, -antis; p. pr.: cf. F. visitant.

visor.etymology: OE. visere, F. visière, fr. OF. vis. See Visage, Vision.

vista.etymology: It., sight, view, fr. vedere, p. p. visto, veduto, to see, fr. L. videre, visum. See View, Vision.

visual.etymology: L. visualis, from visus a seeing, sight: cf. F. visuel. See Vision.

vital.etymology: F., fr. L. vitalis, fr. vita life; akin to vivere to live. See Vivid.

vitellus.etymology: L., the yolk of an egg.

vitiate.etymology: L. vitiatus, p. p. vitiare to vitiate, fr. vitium a fault, vice. See Vice a fault.

vitiligo.etymology: L., a kind of tetter, fr. vitium blemish, vice.

vitreous.etymology: L. vitreous, from vitrum glass; perhaps akin to videre to see (see Vision). Cf. Varnish.

vitrify.etymology: F. vitrifier; L. vitrum glass + -ficare to make. See Vitreous, -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

vitriol.etymology: F. vitriol; cf. Pr. vitriol, vetriol, Sp. & Pg. vitriolo, It. vitriuolo; fr. L. vitreolus of glass, vitreus vitreous. See Vitreous.

vituperate.etymology: L. vituperatus, p. p. of vituperare to blame, vituperate; vitium a fault + parare to prepare. See Vice a fault, and Pare, v. t.

vituperation.etymology: L. vituperatio: cf. OF. vituperation. See Vituperate.

vivacious.etymology: L. vívax, -acis, fr. vivere to live. See Vivid.

vivarium.etymology: L., fr. vivarius belonging to living creatures, fr. vivus alive, living. See Vivid.

vivid.etymology: L. vividus, from vivere to life; akin to vivus living. See Quick, a., and cf. Revive, Viand, Victuals, Vital.

vivify.etymology: F. vivifier, L. vivificare. See Vivid, -fy; cf. Vivificate.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

viviparous.etymology: L. viviparus; vivus alive + parere to bear, bring forth. Cf. Viper.

vivisection.etymology: L. vivus alive + E. section: cf. F. vivisection. See Vivid, and Section.

vixen.etymology: AS. fixen a she-fox, for fyxen, fem. of fox. See Fox.

vizier.etymology: Ar. wezir, wazir, properly, a bearer of burdens, a porter, from wazara to bear a burden: cf. F. vizir, visir. Cf. Alguazil.

vocable.etymology: L. vocabulum an appellation, designation, name, fr. vocare to call, fr. vox, vocis, a voice, a word: cf. F. vocable. See Voice.

vocabulary.etymology: LL. vocabularium, vocabularius: cf. F. vocabulaire. See Vocable.

vocal.etymology: L. vocalis, fr. vox, vocis, voice: cf. F. vocal. See Voice, and cf. Vowel.

vocalic.etymology: L. vocalis (sc. littera) a vowel. See Vocal, a.

vocation.etymology: L. vocatio a bidding, invitation, fr. vocare to call, fr. vox, vocis, voice: cf. F. vocation. See Vocal.

vocative.etymology: L. vocativus, fr. vocare to call.

vociferate.etymology: L. vociferatus, p. p. vociferari to vociferate; vox, vocis, voice + ferre to bear. See Voice, and Bear to carry.

vogue.etymology: F. vogue a rowing, vogue, fashion, It. voga, fr. vogare to row, to sail; probably fr. OHG. wag to move, akin to E. way. Cf. Way.

voice.etymology: OE. vois, voys, OF. vois, voiz, F. voix, L. vox, vocis, akin to Gr. vac to say, to speak, G. erwähnen to mention. Cf. Advocate, Advowson, Avouch, Convoke, Epic, Vocal, Vouch, Vowel.

void.etymology: OE. voide, OF. voit, voide, vuit, vuide, F. vide, fr. (assumed) LL. vocitus, fr. L. vocare, an old form of vacare to be empty, or a kindred word. Cf. Vacant, Avoid.

volant.etymology: L. volans, -antis, p. pr. of volare to fly: cf. F. volant.

volar.etymology: L. vola the palm of the hand, the sole of the foot.

volatile.etymology: F. volatil, L. volatilis, fr. volare to fly, perhaps akin to velox swift, E. velocity. Cf. Volley.

volcano.etymology: It. volcano, vulcano, fr. L. Vulcanus Vulkan, the god of fire. See Vulkan.

volition.etymology: F., fr. L. volo I will, velle to will, be willing. See Voluntary.

volley.etymology: F. volée; flight, a volley, or discharge of several guns, fr. voler to fly, L. volare. See Volatile.

volt.etymology: F. volte; cf. It. volta. See Vault.

volta.etymology: It. volta a turn, turning, a time. See Volt a tread.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

voluble.etymology: L. volubilis, fr. volvere, volutum, to roll, to turn round; akin to Gr. welle a wave: cf. F. voluble. Cf. F. Well of water, Convolvulus, Devolve, Involve, Revolt, Vault an arch, Volume, Volute.

volume.etymology: F., from L. volumen a roll of writing, a book, volume, from volvere, volutum, to roll. See Voluble.

voluntary.etymology: L. voluntarius, fr. voluntas will, choice, from the root of velle to will, p. pr. volens; akin to E. will: cf. F. volontaire, Of. also voluntaire. See Will, v. t., and cf. Benevolent, Volition, Volunteer.

voluptuary.etymology: L. voluptuarius or voluptarius, fr. voluptas pleasure.

voluptuous.etymology: F. voluptueux, L. voluptuosus, fr. voluptas pleasure, volup agreeably, delightfully; probably akin to Gr. velle to wish. See Voluntary.

volute.etymology: F. volute (cf. It. voluta), L. voluta, from volvere, volutum, to roll. See Voluble.

volution.etymology: Cf. LL. volutio an arch, vault.

volvulus.etymology: NL., fr. L. volvere to turn about, to roll.

vomit.etymology: Cf. L. vomere, vomitum, and v. freq. vomitare. See Vomit, n.

voodooism.etymology: Probably (through Creole French vaudoux a negro sorcerer) fr. F. Vaudois Waldensian, because the Waldenses were accused of sorcery.

voracious.etymology: L. vorax, -acis, fr. vorare to devour; akin to Gr. gar. Cf. Devour.

vortex.etymology: L. vortex, vertex, -icis, fr. vortere, vertere, to turn. See Vertex.

vorticella.etymology: NL., dim. fr. L. vortex. See Vortex.

votary.etymology: From L. votus, p. p. vovere to vow, to devote. See Vote, Vow.

vote.etymology: L. votum a vow, wish, will, fr. vovere, votum, to vow: cf. F. vote. See Vow.

votive.etymology: L. votivus, fr. votum a vow: cf. F. votif. See Vow.

vouch.etymology: OE. vouchen, OF. vochier to call, fr. L. vocare to call, fr. vox, vocis, voice. See Voice, and cf. Avouch.

vouchsafe.etymology: Vouch + safe, that is, to vouch or answer for safety.

voussoir.etymology: F., akin to voûte an arch, a vault.

vow.etymology: OE. vou, OF. vou, veu, vo, vu, F. v, from L. votum, from vovere, to vow. Cf. Avow, Devout, Vote.

vowel.etymology: F. voyelle, or an OF. form without y, L. vocalis (sc. littera), from vocalis sounding, from vox, vocis, a voice, sound. See Vocal.

voyage.etymology: OE. veage, viage, OF. veage, viage, veiage, voiage, F. voyage, LL. viaticum, fr. L. viaticum traveling money, provision for a journey, from viaticus belonging to a road or journey, fr. via way, akin to E. way. See Way, n., and cf. Convey, Deviate, Devious, Envoy, Trivial, Viaduct, Viaticum.

vulcan.etymology: L. Vulcanus, Volcanus: cf. Skr. ulka a firebrand, meteor. Cf. Volcano.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

vulgar.etymology: L. vulgaris, from vulgus the multitude, the common people; of uncertain origin: cf. F. vulgaire. Cf. Divulge.

vulgarity.etymology: Cf. F. vulgarité, L. vulgaritas the multitude.

vulgate.etymology: NL. vulgata, from L. vulgatus usual, common, p. p. of vulgare to make general, or common, fr. vulgus the multitude: cf. F. vulgate. See Vulgar, a.

vulnerable.etymology: L. vulnerabilis wounding, injurious, from vulnerare to wound, vulnus a wound; akin to Skr. vra: cf. F. vulnérable.

vulpine.etymology: L. vulpinus, from vulpes a fox.

vulture.etymology: OE. vultur, L. vultur: cf. OF. voltour, F. vautour.

vulva.etymology: L. vulva, volva, from volvere to roll.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.
